screens.title: System Security Hardening and Auditing
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we take a practical, tool-focused look at how to harden RHEL systems and establish reliable auditing. You will learn what SELinux does as a mandatory access control layer, how to create narrowly scoped policy modules instead of disabling protections, how to use AIDE to detect file tampering, how auditd records security-relevant events for forensics, and how OpenSCAP helps enforce compliance baselines. Each tool serves a different role: SELinux prevents processes from using resources they shouldn’t, AIDE detects filesystem changes after the fact, auditd provides a searchable event trail, and OpenSCAP measures conformity to a known standard. Together these controls form layered defenses and an evidence trail for incident response. A concrete example we'll carry through the lab is a custom application that writes logs to an unusual directory; you will see how to generate AVC denials, create a targeted policy with audit2allow, and validate the change without weakening system security. Misconceptions to avoid include treating permissive mode as a fix or storing integrity databases on writable system disks without protection. By the end you will be able to apply these tools in a VM or lab and make reasoned choices about when to write policies, when to update baselines, and how to keep logs usable for investigations. What will you protect first on your server?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to skills you must demonstrate on a hardened RHEL system. First, you will configure and troubleshoot SELinux in enforcing and permissive modes so you can diagnose denials and keep enforcement active. For example, you'll use getenforce and setenforce to observe behavior, then create a small module to allow a web-run script to write logs. Second, you will develop and apply custom SELinux policy modules using audit2allow and semodule so exceptions are limited and reviewed rather than disabling protections. Third, you will implement AIDE for filesystem integrity checking: initialize the database, run checks after a known change, and update the baseline only after verification. Fourth, you will configure auditd rules and analyze logs with ausearch and aureport to trace changes to critical files. Each objective includes a short practical lab so you learn the commands and the judgement calls: when to accept a change into the baseline, and when a reported change indicates a compromise. These are operational skills: they combine commands, log review, and cautious policy creation to keep systems secure and auditable.

screens.narratorSegment: These operational objectives map to the hands-on task. screens.title: What SELinux Is and Why It Matters
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux provides mandatory access control that operates on labels called security contexts. Unlike discretionary control where the owner grants access, SELinux policy defines what processes can do regardless of user identity. A context is a short label attached to files, processes, and ports, and policy rules say which contexts may interact. For example, a web server process labeled with a web context can be allowed to bind port 80 and read files with the appropriate file context, but it cannot arbitrarily write to system configuration paths. This restriction prevents classes of privilege escalation when a service is compromised. A common misconception is that SELinux is only for secrecy; instead its primary role is confinement — reducing the impact of exploited services. To examine contexts, use ls -Z for files and ps -Z for processes; to view mode, use getenforce. Modes matter: permissive logs denials without blocking, enforcing blocks and logs, and disabled removes policy checks entirely. Running in permissive temporarily is useful for capturing policy gaps, but leaving SELinux disabled is a significant security risk. A practical example you will use later is a custom script executed by a web server attempting to write to an unusual directory; the generated AVC denials tell you precisely which permission the process lacked and form the starting point for a narrow policy change. Reflect: how would confinement change your reaction to a compromised service?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › SELinux Fundamentals
Definition and core claim
SELinux enforces mandatory access control using security contexts attached to system objects.
Security context
A label that describes the role/type of a file or process; used by policy rules to allow or deny actions.
Modes
Enforcing blocks and logs, permissive logs only, disabled turns off checks.
Commands to inspect
getenforce, setenforce, ls -Z, ps -Z and reading audit.log for AVC denials.
Concrete example
A web-executed script tries to write to /var/log/myapp and SELinux denies the write because the script process lacks a file type mapping for that directory. The denial contains the required permission and source/target contexts, guiding a minimal policy change.
Misconception
Do not confuse permissive with safe operation; permissive is a diagnostic mode to generate denials for policy authoring, not a long-term configuration.
Key Takeaway

SELinux reduces the blast radius of a compromised process by enforcing what contexts may access.

screens.title: Enforcing vs Permissive vs Disabled
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the three SELinux modes helps you diagnose without weakening protection. Enforcing applies policy decisions and logs denials; it is the intended production state. Permissive does not block actions but logs the denials so you can see what would fail under enforcement — it is a temporary diagnostic mode used when authoring policies. Disabled removes policy checks entirely. A common operational pattern is to keep systems in enforcing while using permissive selectively for a targeted process or a policy module. For example, if a web service needs a new capability, switch only that domain to permissive or run the system in permissive briefly during a controlled test to capture AVC entries; then generate a minimal module and return to enforcing. A misconception is to use permissive as a compatibility shortcut; that increases exposure because policy rules are not applied. To check and change modes, use getenforce and setenforce. For persistent configuration, edit /etc/selinux/config. Practical discipline: always review generated. te files from audit2allow to ensure they grant only what is necessary and not blanket permissions. Closing question: when would you accept a policy change into production rather than adjusting the application?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › SELinux Modes
Mode comparison
Know the behavior and use-cases for each mode and the safe workflow to implement policy changes.
Enforcing
Blocks violations and logs AVC denials. Use this in production to enforce confinement.
Permissive
Logs denials without blocking. Use briefly to identify missing policy rules.
Disabled
No policy checks. Avoid in production; it removes important protections.
Safe workflow: reproduce the denial in permissive, gather AVCs, use audit2allow to create a .te and .pp, review the .te to keep grants minimal, then semodule -i to load and return to enforcing.
Common mistake
Never use permissive as a permanent fix. It hides policy gaps and increases risk by allowing actions that would be blocked under enforcement.
Pro Tip

Target permissive at a specific domain when possible, not the entire system, to limit exposure while collecting AVC information.

screens.title: Diagnosing an SELinux Denial
screens.narratorSegment: When a process fails due to SELinux, the audit trail provides the actionable data. The typical diagnosis flow is: reproduce the failure, collect AVC denials from audit. log or use ausearch, generate a candidate policy with audit2allow, manually inspect the. te file to ensure it grants only necessary rights, compile the module into a. pp, load it with semodule -i, and finally verify the service behavior under enforcing. For a concrete example, imagine a web server failing to write to /var/log/myapp. Run the operation while in permissive or ensure AVCs are present in audit. log. Use ausearch -m AVC -ts today to locate the denials and feed them into audit2allow -M myapp_custom, which yields myapp_custom. te and myapp_custom. pp. Do not blindly install policy packages: the. te file is the review point to avoid overly broad rules. After semodule -i myapp_custom. pp, setenforce 1 and re-test. Misconception to avoid: auto-generating and installing without review can create permissions that expand process capabilities beyond what you intended. The core takeaway is that denials are guidance for minimal policy changes, not a license to relax confinement.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Diagnose & Author
Step-by-step process
Reproduce, collect, generate, review, install, verify.
1
Reproduce the failure under permissive or ensure AVC entries exist in /var/log/audit/audit.log.
2
Collect denials using ausearch -m AVC -ts today | audit2allow -M mymodule to generate .te and .pp.
3
Review the .te file to confirm only minimal grants are present, avoiding broad "allow" statements that open more than needed.
4
Install with semodule -i mymodule.pp, return to enforcing, and test the application behavior.
Concrete CLI example
# collect AVCs and create module
ausearch -m AVC -ts today | audit2allow -M myapp_custom
# review myapp_custom.te, then install
sudo semodule -i myapp_custom.pp
# verify
sudo setenforce 1
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Key Takeaway

Use AVCs as a precise guide to craft minimal policy changes and always inspect generated policy before loading.

screens.title: AIDE — Filesystem Integrity Checking
screens.narratorSegment: AIDE is a filesystem integrity checker that records attributes of files to a baseline database and then reports on any deviations. Attributes can include permissions, owner, size, timestamps, and checksums like md5 or sha256 depending on configuration. The workflow is simple but vital: initialize the database on a known-good system with aide --init, move the generated /var/lib/aide/aide. db. new. gz into place, run scheduled checks with aide --check, review reported differences, and update the baseline with aide --update only after confirming changes are legitimate. An attacker who can modify the system might also try to alter the AIDE database, so storing the baseline on read-only media or off-system is a common best practice. For example, after a package update or legitimate configuration change, AIDE will report modified files; you must verify that changes match the expected maintenance and then update the database. A common mistake is treating AIDE alerts as noise and not investigating timestamps and related logs. The key point is that AIDE provides a forensic comparison to a trusted snapshot; when unexpected modifications are reported, treat them as potential compromise until proven otherwise. How will you protect your baseline in production?

keyIdea.title: Baseline and verify
keyIdea.text: AIDE compares current filesystem state to a trusted baseline; protect the baseline and verify reported changes before updating.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › AIDE Basics
What AIDE records
Attributes include ownership, permissions, size, timestamps, and cryptographic checksums. The configuration /etc/aide.conf controls monitored paths and attributes.
Initialize
sudo aide --init then move the generated aide.db.new.gz into /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz.
Check
sudo aide --check to compare current state to the baseline and produce a report of differences.
Update
If changes are verified legitimate, update the database with sudo aide --update and replace the baseline after review.
Operational note
Run AIDE regularly via cron or scheduler and keep the database off the writable root filesystem if possible. If the baseline is writable by an attacker, alerts are less trustworthy.
Key Takeaway

AIDE is your forensic comparator. Treat unexpected changes seriously and preserve evidence when compromise is suspected.

screens.title: AIDE Demo: Init, Check, Update
screens.narratorSegment: In this demo you will see the AIDE lifecycle in action. Begin by running aide --init on a known-good image; this creates a new database file that you then move into place. Next, perform a small, intentional and documented change such as appending an entry to /etc/hosts. Run aide --check and review the output: AIDE will list modified files and the attributes that changed. Confirm that your planned change is reflected. If the change is legitimate, run aide --update to create an updated database, and then move the new database into the canonical location. A common operational safeguard is to keep a copy of the baseline on read-only media or an external secure store so an attacker cannot trivially overwrite it. AIDE outputs are not self-explanatory in all cases, so correlate timestamps and package-management logs to distinguish legitimate updates from suspicious edits. Misconception: updating the AIDE database immediately on any detected change hides an attacker; only update after verification. As you follow the commands, notice how the report maps to file attributes and how that mapping helps you decide whether to escalate to incident response or simply accept and update the baseline.

keyIdea.title: AIDE lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Initialize a trusted baseline, validate detected differences, and update the baseline only after verification.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › AIDE Demo
Demo steps and commands
Run these in a VM. The code panel below shows the essential sequence; do not run in production without a backup.
# initialize AIDE baseline
dsudo aide --init
sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz

# make a small legitimate change
sudo sh -c 'echo "192.168.1.100 mytestserver" >> /etc/hosts'

# run AIDE check
sudo aide --check

# after verification, update baseline
sudo aide --update
sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz
When reviewing aide --check output, focus on unexpected ownership, checksum or timestamp changes. Correlate with package and system logs to determine cause.
Practical safeguard
Store the AIDE database on read-only media or an isolated management server and run checks frequently via scheduled tasks so changes are detected promptly.
Common Mistake

Updating the baseline without verification can mask an intrusion. Always validate before updating.

screens.title: auditd — Capture Events for Forensics
screens.narratorSegment: auditd is the Linux Audit Daemon that records detailed, security-relevant events. Its strength is recording actions at a kernel level so you can later search events by key, syscall, path, or user. Rules live under /etc/audit/rules. d and can be added dynamically with auditctl. For example, to monitor all writes to /etc/passwd you can add a watch: auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes. The -k flag assigns a key to those events, simplifying searches with ausearch -k passwd_changes and summaries with aureport. A common pitfall is creating overly broad rules that generate enormous volumes of logs. Effective auditing is targeted: choose critical files, sensitive syscall classes, or user sessions that indicate privilege changes. Log rotation and storage planning are also crucial because audit logs can grow quickly; failing to rotate logs risks disk exhaustion. For incident response, auditd records can show who performed an action and when, providing timelines you can correlate with AIDE findings and system logs. Misconception: auditd is not a replacement for AIDE or SELinux; it complements them by preserving an event trail for analysis. Think of auditd as your chronological detective — where did the change happen and which user or process executed it?

keyIdea.title: Targeted, searchable logging
keyIdea.text: Use auditd rules with keys to record and later search for security-relevant events without overwhelming storage.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › auditd Fundamentals
What auditd records and how
auditd captures kernel-level events and writes them to /var/log/audit/audit.log. Rules specify what to record and keys simplify searching.
Example rule
auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k user_auth_changes will log writes and attribute changes to /etc/passwd under the given key.
Search tools
Use ausearch -k user_auth_changes to find events and aureport for summaries and reports.
Operational caution
Design rules narrowly to avoid excessive noise and ensure log rotation to prevent disk exhaustion.
Concrete CLI
# watch /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k user_auth_changes
auditctl -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k user_auth_changes
# list rules
sudo auditctl -l
# search
sudo ausearch -k user_auth_changes -i
Key Takeaway

Use keys and focused rules so you can efficiently find the events that matter during investigations.

screens.title: Audit Log Analysis and Forensic Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Analyzing audit logs requires a methodical approach: identify relevant keys, extract events with ausearch, convert timestamps to a timeline, and correlate with AIDE and system logs. Start by running ausearch -k the_key -i to retrieve human-readable entries. Look for process IDs, executables, and user IDs associated with suspicious events. If you see unexpected writes to system binaries or authentication files, elevate the response: isolate the host, preserve disk images, and avoid reusing the compromised machine for investigation. A common misstep is modifying the system during analysis; do not update baselines or reinstall packages until you have captured evidence. For routine investigation, aureport provides summaries that quickly surface the most frequent rules and hosts. A concrete example: after adding an auditctl rule for /etc/passwd, change a password and run ausearch -k user_auth_changes to confirm the event records the user and timestamp. This link between action and log proves who did what and when. Always cross-check auditd entries with AIDE reports and journalctl to build a consistent incident timeline. Final reflective question: what earlier indicator would you look for to detect tampering sooner?

keyIdea.title: Correlate logs to act
keyIdea.text: Use ausearch and aureport to construct timelines, then correlate with AIDE and journal logs before deciding to isolate or rebuild a host.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Audit Analysis
Analysis pattern
Search with keys, extract events, build a timeline, correlate with AIDE and system logs, then decide containment or recovery.
# search events by key (human readable)
sudo ausearch -k user_auth_changes -i

# summarize audit events
sudo aureport -k --summary

# correlate a timestamp with journalctl
sudo journalctl --since "2026-01-01 10:00" --until "2026-01-01 11:00"
When multiple tools show a change at the same time, that strengthens the evidence. If modifications are unexpected, isolate the host and preserve disk images before remediation.
Concrete example
After adding an audit rule for /etc/passwd, changing a password should appear in ausearch with the acting user and timestamp. This proves who made the change and when.
Common Mistake

Altering files or baselines before preserving evidence can destroy forensic traces. Capture logs and images first.

screens.title: SELinux Live Policy Generation — Lab Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough mirrors the live coding segment. Start with a controlled test that causes an AVC denial: e. g., a web-executed script that tries to write to /var/log/myapp. Temporarily set SELinux to permissive for the whole system or target the web domain so the operation completes while AVCs are logged. Use ausearch -m AVC -ts today to gather AVCs and pipe them to audit2allow -M myapp_custom. Audit2allow produces myapp_custom. te and myapp_custom. pp. Inspect myapp_custom. te carefully to confirm each allow line is minimal and scoped to the specific source and target types. If the. te grants only the necessary operations, install it with semodule -i myapp_custom. pp and return SELinux to enforcing. Validate by running the web action again and checking that no new AVC denials appear. A common misconception is to accept every audit2allow suggestion without inspection. The. te is your opportunity to limit policy expansions. As a concrete judgement, prefer granting file write access to the specific log directory with the correct type rather than permitting broad network or process capabilities. After this exercise, ask yourself: did the new policy precisely match the denied action or did it over-approximate permissions?

keyIdea.title: From AVC to trusted module
keyIdea.text: Generate a candidate policy from AVCs, inspect the .te to ensure minimal grants, then deploy the .pp and verify under enforcing.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Live Policy Lab
Live coding sequence
Follow the commands in a VM and inspect the generated policy before installing.
# cause denials (example)
sudo setenforce 0
# run the web action that writes to /var/log/myapp
# collect AVCs and create module
sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts today | audit2allow -M myapp_custom
# inspect myapp_custom.te
less myapp_custom.te
# install if acceptable
sudo semodule -i myapp_custom.pp
sudo setenforce 1
# verify no new denials
sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts today
When reviewing the .te file, check that allow rules reference the process type and specific file type rather than introducing generic permissions. This keeps the policy minimal.
Misconception check
Do not treat the .pp as trusted without a manual review of the .te. Auto-generated policies can be permissive by default.
Key Takeaway

Audit-driven policy generation speeds fixes but demands human review to maintain a minimal security posture.

screens.title: OpenSCAP — Compliance Scanning and Reports
screens.narratorSegment: OpenSCAP implements SCAP-based assessments that let you evaluate RHEL systems against predefined security baselines. Use oscap xccdf eval with a selected profile from the SCAP content to generate a detailed report showing rules that passed, failed, or were not applicable. For example, running sudo oscap xccdf eval --profile standard --report report. html /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg/content/ssg-rhel8-ds. xml produces an H T M L report that lists each rule, its result, and remediation guidance. OpenSCAP is valuable for evidence during audits and for catching configuration drift in fleets. A common operational approach is to integrate oscap scans into CI/CD pipelines so images are validated before deployment. Be cautious with automated remediation features; automatic fixes can change behaviors and should be tested thoroughly. When interpreting results, prioritize high-severity failures and cross-check with your SELinux and auditd settings to ensure a consistent posture. Misconception: a passing OpenSCAP report does not eliminate the need for runtime protections like SELinux and auditd; it only shows configuration compliance at scan time. The closing reflection: how would you balance automated remediation with safe testing in your environment? OpenSCAP — Compliance Scanning and Reports means openscap evaluates settings against baselines and produces reports useful for audits and ci/cd gating; use remediation carefully and test thoroughly.. In practical terms, assessing a system against a security baseline. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › OpenSCAP Scanning
Scan and report workflow
Choose a profile, run oscap eval, review the HTML report, and plan remediations with testing and change control.
# example scan (RHEL 8 SCAP content)
sudo oscap xccdf eval --profile standard --report report.html /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg/content/ssg-rhel8-ds.xml
# open report.html locally to review pass/fail and remediation guidance
Integrate scans into image pipelines so instances meet baseline requirements before deployment. Treat automated remediation as a last step after validation in staging environments.
Practical caution
OpenSCAP reports are snapshots. Use them in combination with runtime controls and audit logs to form a continuous security picture.
Key Takeaway

Use OpenSCAP for baseline measurement and CI gating, but test remediations thoroughly before applying in production.

screens.title: System Hardening Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Hardening is a collection of practices that complement the specialized tools we've covered. Start with user and password policies: enforce pam_pwquality, set strong complexity and history rules, and require least privilege for accounts. Secure services by disabling unneeded units with sudo systemctl disable --now and lock down SSH with PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no when using keys. Keep systems patched regularly with sudo dnf update. Combine these operational controls with SELinux enforcing, AIDE integrity checks, and targeted auditd rules. A useful way to think about hardening is as layers: baseline configuration and patching, runtime enforcement with SELinux, detection with AIDE and auditd, and compliance checks with OpenSCAP. A common mistake is focusing only on one layer — for example, patching without runtime confinement or logging leaves you blind to misuse after updates. Practical example: when adding a new service, ensure it runs as an unprivileged user, has the minimum capabilities, and is constrained by SELinux types and audit rules. The final reflective question: which layer would you improve first on a service that handles sensitive data? System Hardening Best Practices means combine user policies, minimal services, selinux enforcement, integrity checks, and audit rules for robust hardening.. In practical terms, layered operational controls and everyday configuration choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Combine user policies, minimal services, SELinux enforcement, integrity checks, and audit rules for robust hardening.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Hardening Practices
Operational hardening checklist
Apply the principle of least privilege, disable unnecessary services, enforce strong passwords, and automate patch management.
User policy
pam_pwquality settings, locked privileged accounts, and role separation.
Service security
Disable unused units and run services with minimal capabilities and accounts.
Runtime enforcement
Keep SELinux in enforcing and use targeted policies for exceptions.
Detection & logging
AIDE for integrity, auditd for events, and log rotation to sustain operations.
Example
When introducing a new web service, run it as an unprivileged user, ensure SELinux types map to its files, add an auditd rule for sensitive config files, and include it in OpenSCAP scans.
Key Takeaway

Hardening is layered work: apply small, reviewed changes across configuration, enforcement, detection, and compliance for resilient systems.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Full Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: This guided lab ties all prior concepts into a single workflow. Step one: prepare a VM and install necessary packages such as policycoreutils-python-utils, setroubleshoot-server, aide, and audit. Create /opt/myapp and a small executable that writes to /var/log/myapp to intentionally cause SELinux denials. Temporarily set SELinux permissive, execute the script, then gather AVC entries. Use audit2allow -M to create a candidate module, review the. te file, then semodule -i to install and return to enforcing to confirm correct behavior. Step two: initialize AIDE on the fresh VM with aide --init, then simulate a legitimate configuration change like appending to /etc/hosts. Run aide --check to observe reported differences and then aide --update after verifying the change. Step three: add auditd watch rules for /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow using auditctl -w..., perform a password change, and search the logs with ausearch -k to confirm capture. Throughout, document every change and keep the AIDE baseline and audit logs protected. The lab enforces a discipline: generate evidence, review artifacts, and apply minimal, reviewed changes. After completing these steps, reflect on how the three tools give you prevention, detection, and forensic capability.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three core concepts summarize the chapter. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we take a practical, tool-focused look at how to harden RHEL systems and establish reliable auditing. You will learn what SELinux does as a mandatory access control layer, how to create narrowly scoped policy modules instead of disabling protections, how to use AIDE to detect file tampering, how auditd records security-relevant events for forensics, and how OpenSCAP helps enforce compliance baselines. Each tool serves a different role: SELinux prevents processes from using resources they shouldn’t, AIDE detects filesystem changes after the fact, auditd provides a searchable event trail, and OpenSCAP measures conformity to a known standard. Together these controls form layered defenses and an evidence trail for incident response. A concrete example we'll carry through the lab is a custom application that writes logs to an unusual directory; you will see how to generate AVC denials, create a targeted policy with audit2allow, and validate the change without weakening system security. Misconceptions to avoid include treating permissive mode as a fix or storing integrity databases on writable system disks without protection. By the end you will be able to apply these tools in a VM or lab and make reasoned choices about when to write policies, when to update baselines, and how to keep logs usable for investigations. What will you protect first on your server?

These learning objectives map to skills you must demonstrate on a hardened RHEL system. First, you will configure and troubleshoot SELinux in enforcing and permissive modes so you can diagnose denials and keep enforcement active. For example, you'll use getenforce and setenforce to observe behavior, then create a small module to allow a web-run script to write logs. Second, you will develop and apply custom SELinux policy modules using audit2allow and semodule so exceptions are limited and reviewed rather than disabling protections. Third, you will implement AIDE for filesystem integrity checking: initialize the database, run checks after a known change, and update the baseline only after verification. Fourth, you will configure auditd rules and analyze logs with ausearch and aureport to trace changes to critical files. Each objective includes a short practical lab so you learn the commands and the judgement calls: when to accept a change into the baseline, and when a reported change indicates a compromise. These are operational skills: they combine commands, log review, and cautious policy creation to keep systems secure and auditable.

These operational objectives map to the hands-on task. You will practice switching SELinux modes safely, capture AVC denials, and produce a policy package with audit2allow and semodule. In the AIDE task you will initialize the database, create a small legitimate change, run a check to confirm the detection, and then update the baseline after validation. For auditd you will add fine-grained rules to monitor writes and attribute changes to authentication files and then use ausearch to extract the related events. Each objective stresses a critical decision: when a change should be accepted into a trusted baseline, when a policy should be widened, and when a suspected tampering event requires isolation and forensic preservation. For example, if AIDE reports an unexpected change to a system binary, the correct response includes isolating the host and preserving evidence rather than immediately updating the baseline. These skills help you operate securely in cloud and DevOps environments where automated configurations and CI/CD pipelines may introduce frequent but legitimate changes.

SELinux provides mandatory access control that operates on labels called security contexts. Unlike discretionary control where the owner grants access, SELinux policy defines what processes can do regardless of user identity. A context is a short label attached to files, processes, and ports, and policy rules say which contexts may interact. For example, a web server process labeled with a web context can be allowed to bind port 80 and read files with the appropriate file context, but it cannot arbitrarily write to system configuration paths. This restriction prevents classes of privilege escalation when a service is compromised. A common misconception is that SELinux is only for secrecy; instead its primary role is confinement — reducing the impact of exploited services. To examine contexts, use ls -Z for files and ps -Z for processes; to view mode, use getenforce. Modes matter: permissive logs denials without blocking, enforcing blocks and logs, and disabled removes policy checks entirely. Running in permissive temporarily is useful for capturing policy gaps, but leaving SELinux disabled is a significant security risk. A practical example you will use later is a custom script executed by a web server attempting to write to an unusual directory; the generated AVC denials tell you precisely which permission the process lacked and form the starting point for a narrow policy change. Reflect: how would confinement change your reaction to a compromised service?

Understanding the three SELinux modes helps you diagnose without weakening protection. Enforcing applies policy decisions and logs denials; it is the intended production state. Permissive does not block actions but logs the denials so you can see what would fail under enforcement — it is a temporary diagnostic mode used when authoring policies. Disabled removes policy checks entirely. A common operational pattern is to keep systems in enforcing while using permissive selectively for a targeted process or a policy module. For example, if a web service needs a new capability, switch only that domain to permissive or run the system in permissive briefly during a controlled test to capture AVC entries; then generate a minimal module and return to enforcing. A misconception is to use permissive as a compatibility shortcut; that increases exposure because policy rules are not applied. To check and change modes, use getenforce and setenforce. For persistent configuration, edit /etc/selinux/config. Practical discipline: always review generated. te files from audit2allow to ensure they grant only what is necessary and not blanket permissions. Closing question: when would you accept a policy change into production rather than adjusting the application?

When a process fails due to SELinux, the audit trail provides the actionable data. The typical diagnosis flow is: reproduce the failure, collect AVC denials from audit. log or use ausearch, generate a candidate policy with audit2allow, manually inspect the. te file to ensure it grants only necessary rights, compile the module into a. pp, load it with semodule -i, and finally verify the service behavior under enforcing. For a concrete example, imagine a web server failing to write to /var/log/myapp. Run the operation while in permissive or ensure AVCs are present in audit. log. Use ausearch -m AVC -ts today to locate the denials and feed them into audit2allow -M myapp_custom, which yields myapp_custom. te and myapp_custom. pp. Do not blindly install policy packages: the. te file is the review point to avoid overly broad rules. After semodule -i myapp_custom. pp, setenforce 1 and re-test. Misconception to avoid: auto-generating and installing without review can create permissions that expand process capabilities beyond what you intended. The core takeaway is that denials are guidance for minimal policy changes, not a license to relax confinement.

AIDE is a filesystem integrity checker that records attributes of files to a baseline database and then reports on any deviations. Attributes can include permissions, owner, size, timestamps, and checksums like md5 or sha256 depending on configuration. The workflow is simple but vital: initialize the database on a known-good system with aide --init, move the generated /var/lib/aide/aide. db. new. gz into place, run scheduled checks with aide --check, review reported differences, and update the baseline with aide --update only after confirming changes are legitimate. An attacker who can modify the system might also try to alter the AIDE database, so storing the baseline on read-only media or off-system is a common best practice. For example, after a package update or legitimate configuration change, AIDE will report modified files; you must verify that changes match the expected maintenance and then update the database. A common mistake is treating AIDE alerts as noise and not investigating timestamps and related logs. The key point is that AIDE provides a forensic comparison to a trusted snapshot; when unexpected modifications are reported, treat them as potential compromise until proven otherwise. How will you protect your baseline in production?

In this demo you will see the AIDE lifecycle in action. Begin by running aide --init on a known-good image; this creates a new database file that you then move into place. Next, perform a small, intentional and documented change such as appending an entry to /etc/hosts. Run aide --check and review the output: AIDE will list modified files and the attributes that changed. Confirm that your planned change is reflected. If the change is legitimate, run aide --update to create an updated database, and then move the new database into the canonical location. A common operational safeguard is to keep a copy of the baseline on read-only media or an external secure store so an attacker cannot trivially overwrite it. AIDE outputs are not self-explanatory in all cases, so correlate timestamps and package-management logs to distinguish legitimate updates from suspicious edits. Misconception: updating the AIDE database immediately on any detected change hides an attacker; only update after verification. As you follow the commands, notice how the report maps to file attributes and how that mapping helps you decide whether to escalate to incident response or simply accept and update the baseline.

auditd is the Linux Audit Daemon that records detailed, security-relevant events. Its strength is recording actions at a kernel level so you can later search events by key, syscall, path, or user. Rules live under /etc/audit/rules. d and can be added dynamically with auditctl. For example, to monitor all writes to /etc/passwd you can add a watch: auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes. The -k flag assigns a key to those events, simplifying searches with ausearch -k passwd_changes and summaries with aureport. A common pitfall is creating overly broad rules that generate enormous volumes of logs. Effective auditing is targeted: choose critical files, sensitive syscall classes, or user sessions that indicate privilege changes. Log rotation and storage planning are also crucial because audit logs can grow quickly; failing to rotate logs risks disk exhaustion. For incident response, auditd records can show who performed an action and when, providing timelines you can correlate with AIDE findings and system logs. Misconception: auditd is not a replacement for AIDE or SELinux; it complements them by preserving an event trail for analysis. Think of auditd as your chronological detective — where did the change happen and which user or process executed it?

Analyzing audit logs requires a methodical approach: identify relevant keys, extract events with ausearch, convert timestamps to a timeline, and correlate with AIDE and system logs. Start by running ausearch -k the_key -i to retrieve human-readable entries. Look for process IDs, executables, and user IDs associated with suspicious events. If you see unexpected writes to system binaries or authentication files, elevate the response: isolate the host, preserve disk images, and avoid reusing the compromised machine for investigation. A common misstep is modifying the system during analysis; do not update baselines or reinstall packages until you have captured evidence. For routine investigation, aureport provides summaries that quickly surface the most frequent rules and hosts. A concrete example: after adding an auditctl rule for /etc/passwd, change a password and run ausearch -k user_auth_changes to confirm the event records the user and timestamp. This link between action and log proves who did what and when. Always cross-check auditd entries with AIDE reports and journalctl to build a consistent incident timeline. Final reflective question: what earlier indicator would you look for to detect tampering sooner?

This walkthrough mirrors the live coding segment. Start with a controlled test that causes an AVC denial: e. g., a web-executed script that tries to write to /var/log/myapp. Temporarily set SELinux to permissive for the whole system or target the web domain so the operation completes while AVCs are logged. Use ausearch -m AVC -ts today to gather AVCs and pipe them to audit2allow -M myapp_custom. Audit2allow produces myapp_custom. te and myapp_custom. pp. Inspect myapp_custom. te carefully to confirm each allow line is minimal and scoped to the specific source and target types. If the. te grants only the necessary operations, install it with semodule -i myapp_custom. pp and return SELinux to enforcing. Validate by running the web action again and checking that no new AVC denials appear. A common misconception is to accept every audit2allow suggestion without inspection. The. te is your opportunity to limit policy expansions. As a concrete judgement, prefer granting file write access to the specific log directory with the correct type rather than permitting broad network or process capabilities. After this exercise, ask yourself: did the new policy precisely match the denied action or did it over-approximate permissions?

OpenSCAP implements SCAP-based assessments that let you evaluate RHEL systems against predefined security baselines. Use oscap xccdf eval with a selected profile from the SCAP content to generate a detailed report showing rules that passed, failed, or were not applicable. For example, running sudo oscap xccdf eval --profile standard --report report. html /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg/content/ssg-rhel8-ds. xml produces an H T M L report that lists each rule, its result, and remediation guidance. OpenSCAP is valuable for evidence during audits and for catching configuration drift in fleets. A common operational approach is to integrate oscap scans into CI/CD pipelines so images are validated before deployment. Be cautious with automated remediation features; automatic fixes can change behaviors and should be tested thoroughly. When interpreting results, prioritize high-severity failures and cross-check with your SELinux and auditd settings to ensure a consistent posture. Misconception: a passing OpenSCAP report does not eliminate the need for runtime protections like SELinux and auditd; it only shows configuration compliance at scan time. The closing reflection: how would you balance automated remediation with safe testing in your environment? OpenSCAP — Compliance Scanning and Reports means openscap evaluates settings against baselines and produces reports useful for audits and ci/cd gating; use remediation carefully and test thoroughly.. In practical terms, assessing a system against a security baseline. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hardening is a collection of practices that complement the specialized tools we've covered. Start with user and password policies: enforce pam_pwquality, set strong complexity and history rules, and require least privilege for accounts. Secure services by disabling unneeded units with sudo systemctl disable --now and lock down SSH with PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no when using keys. Keep systems patched regularly with sudo dnf update. Combine these operational controls with SELinux enforcing, AIDE integrity checks, and targeted auditd rules. A useful way to think about hardening is as layers: baseline configuration and patching, runtime enforcement with SELinux, detection with AIDE and auditd, and compliance checks with OpenSCAP. A common mistake is focusing only on one layer — for example, patching without runtime confinement or logging leaves you blind to misuse after updates. Practical example: when adding a new service, ensure it runs as an unprivileged user, has the minimum capabilities, and is constrained by SELinux types and audit rules. The final reflective question: which layer would you improve first on a service that handles sensitive data? System Hardening Best Practices means combine user policies, minimal services, selinux enforcement, integrity checks, and audit rules for robust hardening.. In practical terms, layered operational controls and everyday configuration choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This guided lab ties all prior concepts into a single workflow. Step one: prepare a VM and install necessary packages such as policycoreutils-python-utils, setroubleshoot-server, aide, and audit. Create /opt/myapp and a small executable that writes to /var/log/myapp to intentionally cause SELinux denials. Temporarily set SELinux permissive, execute the script, then gather AVC entries. Use audit2allow -M to create a candidate module, review the. te file, then semodule -i to install and return to enforcing to confirm correct behavior. Step two: initialize AIDE on the fresh VM with aide --init, then simulate a legitimate configuration change like appending to /etc/hosts. Run aide --check to observe reported differences and then aide --update after verifying the change. Step three: add auditd watch rules for /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow using auditctl -w..., perform a password change, and search the logs with ausearch -k to confirm capture. Throughout, document every change and keep the AIDE baseline and audit logs protected. The lab enforces a discipline: generate evidence, review artifacts, and apply minimal, reviewed changes. After completing these steps, reflect on how the three tools give you prevention, detection, and forensic capability.

These three core concepts summarize the chapter. First, SELinux is a mandatory access control system that confines processes via security contexts; prefer enforcing and use permissive only to author targeted policy modules. Second, AIDE provides a trusted baseline for filesystem integrity checks — initialize on a known-good state, verify reported changes, and protect the database from tampering. Third, auditd records kernel-level events you can search with keys using ausearch and summarize with aureport; define narrow rules to capture important actions without overwhelming storage. Together these controls create prevention, detection, and evidence for incident response. Keep in mind that OpenSCAP measures configuration compliance but does not replace runtime protections. Apply the principle of least privilege across users, services, and policies. Finally, always review auto-generated policy suggestions and avoid broad allowances that expand a process’s capabilities unnecessarily. Which of these three will you prioritize in your next system review?

Keep three operational rules in mind as you work: always prefer enforcing SELinux and only create minimal policy exceptions; treat AIDE reports as potential indicators of compromise until verified and protect your baseline; and design auditd rules with keys to make searches effective without producing unmanageable volumes. OpenSCAP gives you a compliance snapshot but does not substitute for runtime controls. In practice, when you see an AIDE change, check auditd and journal entries to build a timeline before deciding to update baselines. When you see an AVC denial, capture it in permissive and then author a targeted policy rather than turning SELinux off. These habits make your systems both resilient and auditable. Which action will you take first to improve the security posture of your next server image? What to Remember means enforce selinux, protect aide baselines, and keep audit rules focused for meaningful logs.. In practical terms, compact reminders for operational action.
